item.title: Compatibility
item.description:
Release Compatibility#

This shows the compatibility of materialize-monitoring with various technologies.

It is also where changes we absorb from outside this repo are recorded — a Materialize metric rename, a Grafana schema bump, an upstream chart moving a value. For what we guarantee about our own names, and the notice you get before one changes, see Stability Guarantees and Deprecation Policy.

materialize-terraform-self-managed#

materialize-terraform-self-managed materialize-monitoring Clouds Observability default
v11.0.0+ 0.17.0 AWS, GCP, Azure On — enable_observability defaults to true
v10.0.0 – v10.1.1 0.12.0 – 0.15.0 AWS, GCP, Azure Off — opt-in
≤ v9.0.2 none (a vendored copy of the env-top dashboard only) — —

The Terraform module ships inside the materialize-monitoring component rather than on a version stream of its own, so one number covers both: a module ref of materialize-monitoring/vX.Y.Z installs chart X.Y.Z. There is no mapping to maintain between the two.

item.title: Stability Guarantees and Deprecation Policy
item.description:
Stability Guarantees and Deprecation Policy#

This page describes which parts of materialize-monitoring you can rely on, and how the project retires an interface before it changes.

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.

Semantic artifact versioning#

This repository publishes several release artifacts, and each one carries its own SemVer version. An artifact bumps its version for the following kinds of change:

item.title: Common Alerts
item.description:
Common Alerts#

These are the alerting rules the chart bundles, generated from the query registry. Each is installed only where the deployment has the capabilities it requires, and only the default set installs without being selected; see Configuring Alerting.

Rules outside the default set have not all been checked against a self-managed install. Evaluate one against the deployment before relying on it.

dev-alerts#

Alerting rules for development awareness.

Each alert here is a condition the stack has already contained: nothing is down, and there is nothing for whoever runs the deployment to fix right now. The people who can remove the cause are the ones who write the software emitting it.

item.title: Common Queries
item.description:
Common Queries#

These queries are used in various dashboards and may be a good starting point for a dashboard developer or for someone looking into particulars of a dashboard.

The underlined values in each query are placeholders, and they are editable. Click one, type your environment’s value, and every other occurrence of that placeholder on the page follows — so copying a query gives you something you can paste straight into Prometheus. Press Enter to commit an edit or Escape to discard it.

You can also set placeholders up front by naming them in this page’s URL:

?mzSqlPrefix=v2_mz_&mzNamespaceList=materialize-prod

The two directions are the same mechanism: editing in place rewrites the URL to match, so once the page reads the way you want, the address bar holds a link you can bookmark or share. Only placeholders you have changed appear there, and a customized value is underlined with a solid rather than a dashed line. Reload without the query string to get the defaults back.

item.title: List of Metrics
item.description:
List of Metrics#

This has the list of metrics which are available for usage. In many systems, only a subset of metrics get stored based on how they would be used.

Metric Tiers#

Importance is about storage, not stability: it says which metrics are worth keeping when capacity is limited, not what we promise about their names. For that, see Stability Guarantees and Deprecation Policy — in short, mz_* names come from Materialize itself and we disclose rather than freeze them.

item.title: Recorded Series
item.description:
Recorded Series#

These are the series the chart’s recording rules write, generated from the query registry. A recorded series is a metric name this repository mints, so it reads the same whatever produced the measurement underneath it. The Thanos ruler evaluates the rules and writes the results back through the alloy-gateway, so a recorded series is queryable wherever the gateway’s other metrics are.

Every ext:* series is part of the normalized layer for an external dependency. One name is recorded by each adapter that can measure it, and the flavor label names the adapter.

item.title: Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)
item.description:
Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs)#

Kubernetes Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) extend the Kubernetes API with custom resources that can be managed with standard Kubernetes tooling. materialize-monitoring both reads custom resources — to decide what to scrape — and creates them — to provision Grafana, its datasources, and its dashboards. Either way the definitions have to exist before the main chart installs, which is why they ship in a chart of their own.

item.description:
materialize-monitoring Changelog#

mzmon-lib (shared library) v0.16.0 (Unreleased)#

Changes Pending

Container Images v0.10.0 (Unreleased)#

Changes Pending

mzmon-lib (shared library) v0.15.0#

  • Give recorded series and ALERTS a metric tier of their own
    • materialize-monitoring#665
    • Recorded series and ALERTS have metric tiers, so a destination below minMetricImportance: all receives them: ALERTS and ext:consensus_up at essential, and the other ext:consensus_* series at recommended.
      • The metrics a recording rule reads keep their own tier. The Thanos ruler reads them from the bundled Thanos, so keep the thanos destination at a tier that includes them. The render warns when it doesn’t.
  • Keep Cargo.lock in step with workspace version bumps
    • materialize-monitoring#664
  • Fold the Karpenter dashboard into Infrastructure Autoscaling
    • materialize-monitoring#660
    • Breaking: Removed: the Karpenter dashboard, infra-karpenter (mz-mon-infra-karpenter). Its panels are on Infrastructure Autoscaling (mz-mon-infra-autoscaling), as a Karpenter row on Overview, Node Pools, Pending Pods, and Cloud Capacity, and a new Karpenter tab.
      • No deprecation cycle: the dashboards component is pre-1.0, and no environment uses this dashboard yet.
      • A selected that names only infra-karpenter now matches nothing, which the chart refuses as a likely typo. Listed beside other stems, it is ignored.
      • Unchanged: mz-mon-infra-autoscaling keeps its name and folder, and every panel it already had.
    • Karpenter’s counters and histograms read over the selected time range, as counts and percentiles, rather than as rates; the Events tab says when each thing happened.
    • Ten Karpenter metrics leave the extended metric tier because no panel reads them: karpenter_cloudprovider_duration_seconds_bucket, karpenter_cluster_utilization_percent, karpenter_nodes_allocatable, karpenter_nodes_current_lifetime_seconds, karpenter_scheduler_queue_depth, karpenter_scheduler_scheduling_duration_seconds_bucket, karpenter_voluntary_disruption_consolidation_timeouts_total, karpenter_voluntary_disruption_decisions_total, karpenter_voluntary_disruption_eligible_nodes, and leader_election_master_status.
      • A destination filtered at extended stops receiving them. The bundled Thanos receives every metric and is unaffected.
  • Update Rust crate zip to v9.2.0
    • materialize-monitoring#659
    • v9.2.0
  • Add the Materialize Ingress dashboard, and scrape the console
    • materialize-monitoring#607
    • Add the Materialize Ingress (Balancer, Console) dashboard (env-ingress)
      • Rate, errors, and latency for each hop users take into an environment: the cloud load balancer, balancerd, the console, and environmentd’s SQL and HTTP APIs. Installed by default with materialize-monitoring-dashboards.
      • The Load Balancer tab draws what AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure reports about the load balancer in front of the environment, when pipeline.metrics.provider pulls it. Without a pull, the tab says how to add one.
      • The Balancer tab also shows balancerd’s CPU and memory and, where a HorizontalPodAutoscaler scales it, the autoscaler’s replicas, targets, and events.
      • balancerd’s latency and server-side error panels need Materialize v26.50.0, and every console panel needs v26.49.0. On older versions they say so, and the SQL and HTTP API tab is unaffected. See Compatibility.
    • Scrape the console’s request metrics (mz_console_*)
      • A new PodMonitor collects them from each console pod’s internal-http port. Configure it under materialize.console.serviceMonitor, the same shape as materialize.balancerd.serviceMonitor.
      • If you upgrade the Materialize operator before an environment, that environment’s console scrape fails (up is 0) until the environment is upgraded too. Set materialize.console.serviceMonitor.enabled to false to skip it for that window.
      • The classic and Google Cloud Managed Prometheus downloads include a matching console scrape config.
  • Alert on draining nodes, graded by what runs on them, with a runbook
    • materialize-monitoring#640
    • New alerts in the default set for draining nodes, meaning nodes that are cordoned or marked for removal by the cluster autoscaler or Karpenter:
      • materialize-node-draining (notice, after 10m), materialize-node-drain-slow (warning, after 2h), and materialize-node-drain-stuck (critical, after 24h), for each environmentd and clusterd pod on a draining node.
      • node-drain-stuck (warning, after 24h), for draining nodes that run no environmentd or clusterd. It fires a day into a GKE blue-green upgrade’s wait on a node pool that runs no Materialize.
    • A Node drains runbook under Operating > Runbooks covers diagnosing a drain, moving Materialize off a node with a rollout, the GKE, EKS, and AKS node pools, and when to escalate to the node pool’s owner. The new alerts link to it.
  • Regenerate locks
    • materialize-monitoring#652

Dashboards (Helm chart) v0.22.0 (Unreleased)#
